nodes.title: Read this as the OSF preprint

fields.label: Read this as the OSF preprint
fields.value: The canonical asset was built from the 61-page OSF preprint, marked under review, rather than the final journal layout. The publication DOI identifies the later paper; quoted pages and reported numbers here refer to that preprint and can differ from the version of record.

fields.label: Measure reflection without requiring mathematics
fields.value: The numerical CRT can conflate reflection with mathematical ability. This project develops a ten-item verbal measure and evaluates its item properties, reliability, construct/predictive validity and group comparability.

fields.label: Related constructs, weaker numeracy dependence
fields.value: The validation program expects positive relationships with numerical CRT and similar patterns for cognitive abilities, while predicting weaker numeracy dependence. Later studies test diary reflection, receptivity, paranormal beliefs, retest stability and math anxiety. Preregistered Study8 distinguishes no anxiety association from a weaker association.

nodes.title: Item development followed by correlational validation

fields.label: Item development followed by correlational validation
fields.value: Studies1/2 evaluate candidate items; Study3 asks experts about appropriateness. Studies4/5 use lab samples, Study6 an online sample, Study7 recontacts Study6 after two weeks, and Study8 examines numeracy/anxiety. The synthesis reuses earlier data rather than recruiting a ninth sample.

nodes.title: Distinct samples and a dependent retest

fields.label: Distinct samples and a dependent retest
fields.value: Reported samples: Study1 203 Prolific; Study2 252 MTurk; Study3 four experts; Study4 270 university-pool participants; Study5 90 began; Study6 199 recruited/197 retained; Study7 158 returned/155 matched to Study6; Study8 221. These counts should not be summed as independent people because the retest reuses participants.

nodes.title: Ten verbal problems with intuitive wrong answers

fields.label: Ten verbal problems with intuitive wrong answers
fields.value: Candidate verbal problems, familiarity ratings and numerical CRT items support item selection. Experts receive both correct and intuitive answers. The final ten items follow a four-stage reduction from46 generated to26 eligible,12 modeled and10 retained.

nodes.title: Measurement batteries vary by validation question

fields.label: Measurement batteries vary by validation question
fields.value: Studies1/2 complete verbal problems, familiarity, numerical CRT and demographics. Study3 rates appropriateness. Study5 adds14 daily entries after a lab session; Study7 repeats both CRTs after two weeks. These are different measurement workflows rather than a single common experiment loop.

fields.label: Correct, intuitive and criterion responses
fields.value: The project compares verbal/numerical CRT scores, familiarity and content judgments with cognitive measures and real-life diary judgments. Correct-response and intuitive-error scores have distinct coding. Anxiety, numeracy and beliefs are measured traits, not randomized treatments.

nodes.title: Item analysis, correlations and multilevel models

fields.label: Item analysis, correlations and multilevel models
fields.value: Item difficulty, discrimination and factor modeling guide selection. Validation uses correlations and hierarchical regression; diary data use multilevel models. Retest correlations and measurement invariance assess reliability/comparability, and gender differences are synthesized across studies. These tests support measure-level claims rather than uniquely identifying a cognitive mechanism.

fields.label: UK candidate-item study
fields.value: Together with Study2, item analyses selected13 candidates under difficulty/intuitive-response/familiarity criteria, then removed a structurally redundant item; factor modeling ultimately retained10. The first study provides item statistics, not a randomized effect estimate.

fields.label: US candidate-item replication
fields.value: The second sample supplies independent item difficulty/familiarity and discrimination evidence used jointly with the UK sample. Final selection requires acceptable properties in both samples; it is not a separate clinical or intervention validation.

fields.label: Expert agreement is weak
fields.value: The four experts’ inter-coder reliability was below chance, Krippendorff alpha=−.05. Authors treat content judgments cautiously and exclude no item solely on this evidence, qualifying the abstract’s broad content-validity language.

fields.label: Predictive validity has limits
fields.value: Verbal CRT predicts four of six outcomes but not moral reasoning or risk preference; numerical CRT predicts all six. Both add incremental variance to a rational-thinking composite, whose internal consistency is low(alpha=.40). Claims are explicitly about measures, not latent constructs.

nodes.title: Daily reflective style is not predicted

fields.label: Daily reflective style is not predicted
fields.value: The two CRTs correlate r=.53,p<.001. Neither predicts daily decision style (numerical p=.218; verbal p=.756), contrary to hypothesis. Both negatively predict receptivity to pseudo-profound statements (p=.016 and.003).

nodes.title: Paranormal beliefs relate more weakly to verbal CRT

fields.label: Paranormal beliefs relate more weakly to verbal CRT
fields.value: The tests correlate r=.42,p<.001. Both negatively relate to paranormal beliefs; verbal p=.023, numerical p<.001. Their correlation strengths differ (p=.003), with the verbal relationship weaker.

fields.label: High two-week retest correlation
fields.value: Numerical and verbal retest reliabilities are r=.83 and.82, with no significant difference(p=.776). This is the matched follow-up to Study6, not a fresh independent validation sample.

nodes.title: Not independent of anxiety, but less associated

fields.label: Not independent of anxiety, but less associated
fields.value: Verbal CRT still correlates negatively with math anxiety(p=.003), rejecting the no-association hypothesis. Its association is weaker than numerical CRT(p=.005); subjective numeracy correlations are .15 versus.46 and differ(p<.001).

fields.label: Group comparisons and invariance
fields.value: The reported synthesis finds numerical CRT gender difference g=.29,p<.001 but verbal g=−.06,p=.341. Verbal CRT meets the adopted scalar-invariance criteria across gender, age and administration settings. Nonsignificance is not proof of exactly identical population means.

nodes.title: A complementary measure with mixed criterion evidence

fields.label: A complementary measure with mixed criterion evidence
fields.value: The preprint supports a less numeracy-dependent, reliable verbal CRT, but retains null diary predictions, weak expert agreement and remaining anxiety/numeracy associations. These qualifications matter when interpreting broad claims of validation.

fields.label: Familiarity, representativeness and modeling choices
fields.value: Repeated exposure can erode unfamiliarity; criterion coverage is not exhaustive. Samples are nonrepresentative English-speaking adults/students. The authors recommend further item-response analysis and broader samples.

evidence.quote:
Supplementary materials, all datasets and pre-registration for Study 8 are available at
https://osf.io/xehbv/.
Note: This manuscript is currently under review for publication. Please feel free to cite this preprint
until the manuscript is accepted for publication.

The Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) became popular for its impressive power to predict how 
well people reason and make decisions. Despite the popularity of the CRT, a major issue 
complicates its interpretation: the numerical nature of the CRT confounds reflection ability 
with mathematical ability. We have addressed this issue by developing the Verbal CRT (CRT-V), 
a novel 10-item measure of cognitive reflection, using non-mathematical problems with good 
statistical and psychometric properties and with low familiarity. First, we selected suitable items 
with relatively low familiarity and optimal difficulty as identified in two different populations 
(Studies 1 and 2) and with high content validity as judged by an expert panel (Study 3). Second, 
we demonstrated a good criterion and construct validity for the test in different populations 
with a wide range of variables (Studies 4-6, 8) and a good internal consistency and test-retest 
reliability (Study 7). The Verbal CRT was less associated with numeracy than the original CRT 
and it was test equivalent across gender, age groups and administration setting. In contrast with 
the original CRT (Hedge’s g = 0.29, 95% CI[0.17, 0.40]), the Verbal CRT showed no gender 
differences (Hedge’s g = -0.06, 95% CI[-0.18, 0.06]). The Verbal CRT can complement existing 
tests of cognitive reflection.

Study 1. We aimed to recruit at least 200 participants to be able to estimate the difficulty and 
discriminability of the items. A sample of 203 participants recruited from an online panel Prolific 
Academic (54.2% men, age ranged from 18 to 63 years, M = 31.1, SD = 10.2 years) completed 
the online survey. They were paid for their up to 20-minute participation by a flat fee of £2. 
The sample was heterogeneous in terms of education (1% had not finished high school, 30.5% 
had finished high school, 48.3% had an undergraduate degree, 18.2% had a master’s degree and 
2.0% had a doctoral or professional degree) and occupation (27.6% of participants were 
unemployed, homemakers or students, 25.1% were working as managers and professionals, 
9.9% were working in sales and office, 7.4% were working in service and the remaining 30.0% 
were in some other occupation). The study featured a non-experimental design. The blocks of 
26 verbal problems, their familiarity, three numerical problems and their familiarity occurred in 
a fixed order and the items within each block were presented in a randomised order to each 
participant.
Study 2. A sample of 252 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers (55.2% men, age ranged from 19 to 
72 years, M = 36.4, SD = 11.5 years) completed the online survey. They were paid for their up 
to 20-minute participation by a flat fee of $2.40. The sample was heterogeneous in terms of 
education (0.8% had not finished high school, 32.5% had finished high school, 54.8% had an 
undergraduate degree, 10.3% had a master’s degree and 1.6% had a doctoral or professional 
degree) and occupation (24.2% were working as managers and professionals, 17.9% were 
working in sales and office, 17.1% were unemployed, homemakers or students, 12.3% were 
working in service and the remaining 28.5% were in some other occupation). The design was 
the same as in Study 1.

Study 3. An expert panel (n = 4, 2 female and 2 male researchers, age Mdn = 41.5 years) was 
asked to assess the appropriateness of the individual items. The experts had at least 10 years of

research experience since receiving their PhD at the time of assessment (namely, 10, 11, 12 and 
40 years), and they were research active in the area of intuitive and analytical cognitive 
processing as documented by their conference and peer-reviewed journal contributions. The 
study featured a non-experimental design in which the experts assessed the appropriateness of 
the 26 verbal problems presented in a randomised order.
Materials and Procedure. 
Study 1. After providing informed consent, participants completed 26 verbal problems (see 
Appendix), and, in turn, they assessed the familiarity of the 26 verbal problems. Participants 
then completed the three-item version of the numerical Cognitive Reflection Test (Frederick, 
2005) and, in turn, assessed the familiarity of the items using the same question used for the 
verbal problems. They then provided their age, gender, occupation and education level before 
being debriefed. We coded the correct and intuitive answers using an agreed coding scheme 
(see Appendix).
Study 2. The materials and procedure were identical to those in Study 1. 
Study 3. After providing informed consent, the experts assessed the appropriateness of the 26 
verbal problems using a 4-point Likert scale (1: not appropriate, 2: somewhat appropriate, 3: quite 
appropriate and 4: very appropriate). The experts were told that all, some or none of the 26 
items could be considered appropriate. For each item, we provided information describing the 
intuitive (wrong) answer and the correct answer to help the experts to assess the suitability of 
each item. Finally, the experts completed a short socio-demographic section and were 
debriefed. 
Results

Item testing. First, we conducted item-level analyses using the R package ‘psychometric’(Fletcher 
& Fletcher, 2010). In Table 1, we have reported item difficulty (and its standard deviation), item 
discriminability, item-total correlation and item-criterion correlation (where the criterion is the 
Numerical CRT) as well as item’s intuitive responses proportion (i.e., the proportion of wrong 
“intuitive” responses out of all responses) and familiarity for Studies 1 and 2. In Table 1, we 
have also reported the medians of the appropriateness judgments made by the experts in Study 
3. We interpreted these judgments with extreme caution because the inter-coder reliability of 
the experts was not different from a chance level, Krippendorff’s α = -0.05. This evidence was 
always assessed in a context of other supportive evidence; as a matter of fact, none of the items 
was excluded based on this evidence. We nevertheless report these findings here for full 
transparency.
The cut-off points for necessary and supportive criteria for item inclusion in the scale 
were derived from the recommendations in the psychometric literature (AERA, APA, & NCME, 
2014; Furr, 2017; Gregory, 2004). For an item to be included in the Verbal CRT, it had to fulfil 
three necessary criteria: (i) item difficulty should be higher than 20% and lower than 70% in both 
samples, (ii) item intuitive response proportion (i.e., the proportion of the intuitive, incorrect, 
responses) had to be at least 30%, (iii) the initial familiarity of the items should be 40% or 
lower. In addition, we took into account the following supportive evidence when considering 
including the item: (i) experts’ judgment of content validity of the item equal or higher than Mdn
= 3 and item-level content validity index (i-CVi) of .50 or higher (but this was interpreted with 
extreme caution), (ii) discrimination index (i.e., differentiating lower and upper half of 
responses) higher than 0.25, (iii) item-total reliability higher than 0.20, (iv) item-criterion 
correlation higher than 0.10. Based on these criteria we selected 13 items (Table 1). Items 1, 2, 
4, 5, 6, 7, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 22 and 26 fulfilled the necessary conditions and fulfilled additional 
criteria in the supportive evidence category.

To summarise, in the four-stage process, we generated 46 items, 20 of which were 
screened out. Based on the item level analysis, we kept only 12 items out of the 26 eligible 
items. Finally, based on the series of confirmatory factor analysis, we identified 10 items with 
satisfactory loadings. We used the final 10-item version of the Verbal CRT in the subsequent 
studies to assess its construct validity and reliability.

To assess the evidence of the construct validity of the Verbal CRT, we designed an
extensive validation study that we conducted in controlled laboratory conditions. To assess the 
convergent and discriminant validity evidence of the Verbal CRT, we measured cognitive 
reflection (i.e., the Numerical CRT), cognitive ability and executive functions, working memory, 
thinking dispositions and numeracy. Prior research found weak to medium positive correlations 
between cognitive ability, working memory and executive functions, thinking dispositions, 
numeracy and the Numerical CRT (Frederick, 2005; Liberali et al., 2012; Toplak et al., 2011, 
2014; Toplak, West, & Stanovich, 2017). We expected to find similar correlation patterns for 
cognitive ability, working memory, executive functioning and thinking dispositions in terms of 
direction even though not necessarily of the same strength due to numeracy confounding the 
relationships with the Numerical CRT.

Participants and Design. We aimed to recruit at least 258 participants to be able to detect 
at least a weak correlation of r = 0.2, assuming α = .05, 1 - β = .90, and a conservative two￾tailed test (Cohen, 1988; Faul, Erdfelder, Lang, & Buchner, 2007). We also assumed a 5% 
attrition rate (e.g., due to technical issues, incomplete questionnaires, etc.). As a result, 270 
participants (70% female; age ranged from 18 to 62 years, M = 22.3, SD = 5.2 years) took part 
in the study. They were recruited from the University of Essex’s voluntary participation pool. 
Participants were mostly students (86.3%) or they were in other occupations (13.7%).

Verbal CRT significantly predicted four outcome variables (i.e., it did not predict moral 
reasoning and risk preference), whereas the Numerical CRT predicted all six variables. The 
correlations for belief bias and risk preference were significantly lower for the Verbal CRT 
compared with the Numerical CRT. 
To test the incremental validity of the Verbal CRT over and above other cognitive 
processing variables, we ran a series of hierarchical regression analyses, in which all convergent 
and discriminant validity variables (see Table 4) were entered as predictors in a successive and 
structured way to predict a composite rational thinking variable. Aligned with the 
recommendations of Westfall and Yarkoni (2016), we restrict ourselves here to the claims 
concerning the incremental validity of the measures (not constructs), since we do not have
sufficient statistical power to run a set of structural equation models. We developed the 
composite rational thinking variable following the strategy used in prior research (Toplak et al., 
2014). In a subset of complete cases (n = 247), we recoded the four successfully predicted 
outcome variables so that higher scores represented more rational thinking (i.e., reversed 
coded belief bias and denominator neglect), transformed them into z-scores and aggregated 
them into one composite rational thinking variable. The internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 
0.40) of this composite variable was low, but similar to the consistency of such composite 
variables of rational thinking reported in prior research (e.g., Toplak et al., 2011). We 
successively entered the construct validity variables: the initial model consisted of cognitive 
ability variables only (model 1), to which we added the executive function variables (model 2), 
to which we added numeracy (model 3), to which we added thinking disposition variables 
(model 4) and finally we either added the Numerical CRT (model 5A) or the Verbal CRT 
(model 5B). The findings (Table 4) indicate that each block contributed to a significant increase 
in the explained variance except the thinking dispositions block. Critically, adding the Numerical 
CRT or the Verbal CRT contributed significantly to the explained variance, above and beyond

To extend the predictive validity of the Verbal CRT, we conducted an additional lab 
study, in which we focused on (i) decision-making style and (ii) receptivity to profound bullshit 
(Pennycook et al., 2015a). We leveraged a 14-day long diary study to devise a very realistic 
measure of decision-making style, whereby each day people reported their own decisions and 
assessed their reflective or intuitive nature. First, we hypothesised that the Verbal CRT would 
be positively related with the Numerical CRT. Second, we hypothesised that the Numerical 
CRT, as well as the Verbal CRT, would positively predict the reflective style of decision-making. 
Third, we expected that the Numerical CRT and the Verbal CRT would negatively predict the 
higher receptivity to profound bullshit. We did not have any expectations regarding the 
attenuation of the correlation since both variables are relatively unexplored in terms of their 
association with the numerical component of the Numerical CRT.
Method
Participants and design. We aimed to recruit at least 84 participants to be able to 
detect at least a weak correlation of r = -.30, assuming α = .05, 1 - β = .80, and conservatively a 
two-tailed test (Faul et al., 2007). This is a very conservative estimate since we used multilevel 
models, where lower standard errors can be expected, to estimate the relationship between 
the Cognitive Reflection Tests and predicted variables. Initially, 90 participants recruited from a 
student pool commenced the research study by completing a one-hour lab study. This was 
followed up a week later by a 14-day period of daily diary entries.

Materials and procedure. After providing informed consent, participants completed a one￾hour lab study. For the purposes of our study, they completed the 3-item version of the 
Numerical CRT (Frederick, 2005) and the 10-item version of the Verbal CRT. The internal 
consistency for the Numerical CRT was acceptable (Cronbach’s α = 0.77) and good for the 
Verbal CRT (Cronbach’s α = 0.84). The items for both tests were presented in a random 
order. A few days later, participants were invited to complete a set of various tasks in a 14-day 
diary study. For this study, participants were first asked to recall and describe the 
decision/choice of that day and assess their style of deciding on an intuitive-analytical dimension. 
The analytical vs. intuitive decision style was assessed by seven items (e.g., “I weighed up the 
pros and cons before making the decision”). The items were inspired by items found in the 
International Personality Item Pool ("International Personality Item Pool: A Scientific 
Collaboratory for the Development of Advanced Measures of Personality Traits and Other 
Individual Differences.," 2018). Participants provided their judgment on a 5-point Likert scale (1: 
strongly disagree, 2: somewhat disagree, 3: neither agree nor disagree, 4: somewhat agree, 5: strongly 
agree). The scale had a satisfactory internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.78). The average 
score ranged from 1 to 5; higher scores indicated a preference for analytical thinking style. 
Participants assessed their decision/choice every day of the 14 days. We have coded the 
description of the decision – whether the participants described a decision. After removing 22 
duplicate invalid entries, out of 961 decisions, 59 did not describe an actual decision (e.g., 
“none”) and 902 described an actual decision (e.g., “Whether to take a room or not”).

We observed a moderate and statistically significant correlation between the Numerical 
and Verbal CRTs, r = .53, p < .001. This supports the first hypothesis about the construct 
similarity of the Verbal CRT to the Numerical CRT. Contrary to our expectations in the 
second hypothesis, we found that the Numerical and Verbal CRTs did not predict decision￾making style using a multilevel model with random intercept and random slope, nested within 
participants and days, b = -0.06, SE = 0.04, t(50.19) = -1.25, p = .218 and b = 0.01, SE = 0.02, 
t(37.26) = 0.31, p = .756, respectively. The null effect might indicate a true lack of predictive 
power of the CRT measures since the CRT only weakly predicts real-life decisions (e.g., 
Juanchich et al., 2016) or it might reflect methodological issues associated with the new 
measure since it was not validated. However, even though our second hypothesis was not 
confirmed, the prediction patterns between the two tests were very similar (centered around 
zero), which supported similar predictive properties between the Numerical and Verbal CRTs. 
Finally, aligned with our third hypothesis concerning receptivity for profound bullshit, we found 
– using a multilevel model with random intercept and random slope – that the Numerical and 
Verbal CRTs negatively predicted the receptivity to profound bullshit to a similar extent, b = -
0.19, SE = 0.08, t(61.71) = -2.49, p = .016 and b = -0.10, SE = 0.03, t(46.00) = -3.13, p = 0.003,

participants completed the online survey. They were reimbursed for the estimated 12-minute 
participation by a flat fee of £1. Following our a priori exclusion criteria, we excluded two 
participants who did not correctly answer at least two out of three bogus questions (Meade & 
Craig, 2012). None of the participants was excluded due to time exclusion (i.e., completing the 
survey in less than one-third of the median time, Mdn = 13.1). Hence, the final sample was 197 
(56.9% women, age ranged from 18 to 64 years, M = 33.8, SD = 12.3 years). The sample was 
heterogeneous in terms of education (0.5% had not finished high school, 36.0% had finished high 
school, 47.7% had an undergraduate degree, 9.6% had a master’s degree and 6.1% had a 
doctoral or professional degree) and occupation (32.5% were unemployed, homemakers or 
students, 24.9% were working as managers and professionals, 11.2% were working in sales and 
office, 8.1% were working in service and the remaining 23.3% were in some other occupation 
category). The design of the study was correlational.

We observed a moderate and statistically significant positive correlation between the 
Numerical and Verbal CRTs, r = .42, p < .001. Again, this further supports the construct 
similarity of the Verbal CRT with the Numerical CRT. We observed a weak negative 
correlation between the Numerical CRT and paranormal beliefs as well as a weak negative 
correlation between the Verbal CRT and paranormal beliefs (Figure 2). As expected, both 
correlations were in the predicted directions and were both statistically significantly different 
from zero, t(195) = - 5.73, p < .001; t(195) = - 2.29, p = .023, respectively. The correlations 
were similarly weak and alike when using non-parametric Spearman correlations (ρ = -.39 and -
.16, respectively). The correlation of paranormal beliefs with the Numerical CRT, as predicted, 
was larger than the one with the Verbal CRT (Figure 2), z = -2.99, p = .003 (Diedenhofen & 
Musch, 2015). Thus, the Verbal CRT predicted negative paranormal beliefs, similarly to the way 
that the Numerical CRT did, however, the correlation was attenuated.

Participants and design. The Prolific Academic online workers who completed Study 
6 were eligible to participate (n = 197); they were all invited by email to participate in this study 
two weeks after completing Study 6. A sample of 158 participants completed the online survey, 
from which we were able to match 155 participants via their ID number (i.e., three participants 
failed to provide an ID number that could be matched with the original list of IDs). This sample 
size enabled us to detect a weak correlation of r = 0.22, assuming α = .05, 1 - β = .80, and 
conservatively a two-tailed test (Faul et al., 2007). The sample consisted of 56.8% women; age 
ranged from 18 to 64 years, M = 35.1, SD = 12.7 years. The sample was heterogeneous in 
terms of education (37.4% had finished high school, 45.2% had an undergraduate degree, 10.3% 
had a master’s degree and 7.1% had a doctoral or professional degree) and occupation (32.3% 
were unemployed, homemakers or students, 26.5% were working as managers and 
professionals, 9.0% were working in sales and office, 5.2% were working in service and the 
remaining 27.0% were in some other occupation category). The participants were reimbursed 
for the estimated 10-minute participation by a flat fee of £0.85. The design of the study was 
correlational.
Materials and procedure. After providing informed consent, participants solved the 
7-item version of the CRT (Toplak et al., 2014) and the Verbal CRT (10 items). The order of 
presentation of the two tests and the items was randomised. The internal consistency for the 
Numerical CRT was acceptable (Cronbach’s α = 0.75) and good for the Verbal CRT 
(Cronbach’s α = 0.86). Finally, participants completed some socio-demographic questions and 
were debriefed.

We found a moderate and statistically significant positive correlation between the 
Numerical and Verbal CRTs in the second measurement, r = .41, p < .001 (Figure 3). Critically, 
we found that for both the Numerical and Verbal CRTs the performance in test and retest was 
highly correlated and similar in size (r = .83 and .82, respectively, Figure 3), z = 0.28, p = .776 
(using the cocor R package, Diedenhofen & Musch, 2015). Thus, the Verbal CRT had very high 
test-retest reliability, which was virtually identical to the reliability of the Numerical CRT.

Participants and design. We aimed to recruit 221 participants to be able to detect a 
weak correlation of r = 0.2, given α = .05, 1 - β = .80 using a two-tailed test (Faul et al., 2007). 
Participants from the Prolific Academic online panel were eligible to participate if (i) their 
approval rate was at least 95% while having at least two previous submissions, (ii) they were UK 
nationals and (iii) they were 18 years old or older. A sample of 221 participants completed the 
online survey. They were paid £0.85 for the estimated 10-minute participation. Following our a 
priori exclusion criteria, none of the participants was excluded due to time exclusion or 
incompleteness. The participants were mostly women (72.9%) and their ages ranged from 18 to 
71 years, M = 34.7, SD = 12.4 years. The sample was heterogeneous in terms of education 
(0.9% had not finished high school, 40.3% had finished high school, 42.1% had an undergraduate 
degree, 14.5% had a master’s degree and 2.3% had a doctoral or professional degree) and 
occupation (27.1% were working as managers and professionals, 26.2% were unemployed, 
homemakers or students, 9.5% were working in sales and office, 5.0% were retired, 4.5% were 
working in service and the remaining 27.7% were in some other occupation category). The 
design of the study was correlational.

We observed moderate correlations between the Numerical CRT and subjective numeracy and 
math anxiety, while we observed only weak correlations between the Verbal CRT and 
subjective numeracy and math anxiety (Figure 4). We found a statistically significant weak 
negative correlation between the Verbal CRT and math anxiety, t(219)= - 3.02, p = .003 
(disconfirming Hypothesis 1a) and a moderate negative correlation between the Numerical 
CRT and math anxiety, t(219)= - 6.12, p < .001 (supporting Hypothesis 1b). The correlation

with math anxiety was statistically significantly lower for the Verbal CRT than for the Numerical 
CRT, z = 2.83, p = .005 (supporting Hypothesis 1c, using “cocor” package). Thus, the pattern 
was consistent with the weak version of the argument—the Verbal CRT compared with the 
Numerical CRT is much less associated with math anxiety. A similar correlational pattern, was 
observed with subjective numeracy (Figure 4): the correlation with subjective numeracy was 
statistically significantly lower for the Verbal CRT (r = .15) than for the Numerical CRT (r = 
.46), z = -4.92, p < .001 (confirming Hypothesis 2). Thus, we found that math anxiety and 
subjective numeracy were still correlated with the Verbal CRT but only very weakly and 
substantially and significantly less than with the Numerical CRT.

Based on these RMSEA and CFI cutoff criteria, the Verbal CRT demonstrated the most 
stringent, scalar (strong factorial) form of invariance across gender groups, age groups, and 
administration settings (see Table 5). The measurement invariance of the Numerical CRT was 
only tested for gender where it demonstrated scalar invariance (see Table 5).

We found evidence of gender effect in the Numerical CRT: men performed better than 
women, Hedges’ g = 0.29, z = 4.73, p < .001. Importantly, we found no evidence for gender 
difference in the Verbal CRT, Hedges’ g = -0.06, z = -0.95, p = .341 (see Figure 5). The type of 
CRT (numerical vs. verbal) was a statistically significant moderator of the gender difference, 
QM(2) = 33.47, p < .001, supporting that the gender difference was significantly greater for the 
numerical CRT than for the Verbal CRT. The test for residual heterogeneity was not 
statistically significant, QE(8) = 15.88, p = .103. Thus, women did not perform as well as men in 
the Numerical CRT but performed as well as men in the Verbal CRT.

Four limitations of the current research deserve readers’ attention. First, even though 
our items have low initial familiarity, with the continuous use of the measure, familiarity might 
become an issue. Future research should address the issue of previous exposure and its effect 
on predictive validity. Second, even though we used a wide range of measures to test the 
Verbal CRT’s construct validity covering different domains, the list was not exhaustive. Future 
research should, therefore, test other outcome variables and investigate whether the Verbal 
CRT predicts these more or less successfully than the Numerical CRT. Third, we used non￾representative samples of English-speaking participants in our research: university student 
samples and non-random samples from a general adult population. It would be important to 
further establish the robustness of the predictive validity of the Verbal CRT in random samples 
drawn from a general adult population. We believe that our test will be an excellent measure of 
cognitive reflection especially in non-student populations that lack mathematical skills and/or 
suffer from mathematical anxiety. Finally, we adopted here a classical testing theory approach 
when selecting the items for the factor structure phase and item response theory in the factor 
structure phase; the consistent use of the latter approach might have been a better approach 
since it offers many advantages over the traditional approach. It would be important to 
scrutinise the Verbal CRT using the item response theory.
